headline: Cockenoe on the Flood: Bluefish Corner the Bunker, Porgies Steady on the Cows
subhead: With bunker schools pinned against the reef line, the bluefish bite is the sure thing this week — stripers and fluke are the projects.
body_markdown:
The call this week is Cockenoe Reef on the last two hours of the flood, and here's the thinking behind it. Bunker schools have been working the reef complex from the Norwalk Islands east toward Penfield, and with the moon building toward full, tidal flow is picking up enough to pin those schools against structure instead of letting them wander open water. That's exactly the setup bluefish want — bait trapped, current running, an ambush point built right into the rock. Cockenoe sits in 12 to 20 feet with enough relief to hold gamefish underneath moving bait, and it's been the most consistent producer in the zone for the last week and a half.

The thermal picture backs this up. Kings Point is reading 70.9 and New London 69.4, which keeps the classic west-to-east gradient intact — warmer water on our end of the Sound, cooler water building toward the Race. That gradient matters because it means the Western Sound reef system is still holding the most active feeding pattern in Connecticut waters right now, while the eastern stretch cools off first. Bunker density is still the engine driving all of it. The same bait push fueling the bluefish tournament fleet working schools down toward the city line is running right through our reef line too, and it should keep doing so through Labor Day week unless something scatters the bunker.

Bluefish are the reliable target. Cockenoe, the outer edge of the Norwalk Islands, and the flats off Sheffield Island have all been giving up bluefish in the 3 to 6 pound class, mixed with some cocktail-sized fish, on bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig in 15 to 20 feet, and on poppers and metal — Kastmasters and Hopkins — worked over breaking fish when the blitzes show on top. Best window is that last stretch of the flood into the top of the tide, before boat traffic from the weekend crowd pushes fish off the structure. Weekday mornings are quieter and the bite holds longer without six boats circling the same school.

Stripers are still in a holding pattern, and that's not a surprise — we flagged this last week, said nighttime activity would gradually improve on structure as the heat eased off, and that's what the fleet is seeing. Nothing close to a blitz yet, but the Norwalk Islands' back channels and the rock piles off Greenwich Point are giving up scattered fish after dark on the last of the ebb, when warm water draining out of the shallows concentrates bait along the current seams. Bucktails in the 3/4 to 1-ounce range, white or chartreuse, worked slow along the drop-offs, are outproducing anything cast blind into open water. The real push — the one where bait density finally forces stripers to commit in numbers — is still a week or two off. Bunker have to concentrate further first, and that's a process, not a light switch.

Fluke fishing has softened into the pattern you'd expect for the calendar. This is a normal seasonal transition, not a collapse — the channel edges between the Norwalk Islands and the deeper cuts off Sheffield Island are still giving up keeper fish, just fewer of them and more work per fish. Gulp and bucktail combinations, white or pink, dragged slow along bottom in 15 to 25 feet on the last of the outgoing, are the play. Expect this to hold fair through September before the offshore push starts pulling fish out of the Sound entirely.

Penfield Reef is where the bottom bite lives right now. Blackfish are starting to show on the rockpile, still early-season numbers but real fish, and porgies are thick on the Cows off Stamford — hi-lo rigs with sandworm or green crab, fished tight to structure in 10 to 15 feet on the tail end of the ebb when current eases enough to hold bottom without getting swept off the rock. That window is short — maybe 90 minutes around dead low — but it's been productive every day the fleet has worked it this week. Black sea bass are mixing in as bycatch on the same structure, nothing to plan a trip around specifically but a welcome addition to the box.

Looking at the next few days, expect more of the same setup: bluefish the surest bet on the bunker schools working the reef line, best on the flood before weekend boat traffic thickens up. If you've only got one window this weekend, take the early flood at Cockenoe or the islands and get off the water before the Saturday parade of center consoles pushes through — Labor Day weekend traffic is going to be heavy everywhere from Greenwich Point east, and fish that get pressured off structure by 10 a.m. usually don't come back until the pressure lifts. The striper pattern is the one to watch closest. If bait keeps building through the week the way it has, the first real concentration could show along the reef edges by the weekend after next, and that's the window worth clearing the calendar for.
